This section correctly sets forth the primary purpose of the sutra. It consists of three parts: first, a general exposition; second, a summary praising the excellence of the teaching and the profundity of the capacity of the recipients;

and third, a defense against potential objections. The first of these [the general exposition] has two sub-sections: first, a counter-exposition of the arrival of the teaching; and second, a counter-exposition of the ripening of the capacity. The first of these [the arrival of the teaching] is as follows.
Now, as for the descent of spiritual power upon a sacred mountain, it cannot be brought about through transformation unless there is a Great Sage.
The phrase "as for" (*fuyi*) is a rhetorical particle used to introduce the following text; because the subsequent passage shifts its focus, it is repeated here.
It is like clouds appearing before rain, or smoke rising before fire, serving as preceding signs. Thus, Master Wufeng said: "Oily clouds..."

One knows that the rain falls profusely; golden lightning flashes and thunder rolls. Such is the natural course of principle and circumstance. "Numinous Peak" refers to the "Numinous Mountain" (Gṛdhrakūṭa), where [the Buddha] descended.
"Numinous" (*ling*) signifies spiritual brilliance; it is a term for that which transcends the crowd and excels its peers.
It means that within a sandalwood forest, no common trees grow; within a lion’s den, no other beasts enter. As for those of former years who were like withered sprouts or rotten seeds, or the lame...
As for the turtle, the lame donkey—how could they have been invited to this sublime assembly? Therefore, those who descended were all spirits.
"The Great Sage" refers to the present Buddha; because he practices both the provisional and the ultimate, transcending all other sages and standing alone as supreme, he is called "Great.

"Opening" is said in contrast to ordinary beings, meaning he opens up the sealed enclosure of their ignorance. "Transforming" is said in contrast to the followers of the Lesser Vehicle, meaning he transforms their provisional teachings.
Stubborn adherence and lack of means—these all serve to reveal the underlying intent.

It is said that among the eminent and spiritual assembly descended upon Vulture Peak in the past, it was only after forty years of multifaceted refinement by the Great Sage that their sealed barriers could finally be opened.
He transformed their stubborn attachments until they reached this state. Were he not a Great Sage, how could he have been capable of such a thing? Therefore it is said:
"There was no way to open and transform them. △ Second, revealing by contrast that the spiritual capacity had matured.
Regarding the phrase "the reach of appropriate transformation": it is not without past conditions that the mind can be guided;

this refers to what is "appropriate. "Transformation" (*hua*) points to the present sutra; "reach" (*ji*) means to be affected by it. "Past conditions" (*xi yuan*) refers to those such as Jñānavijaya and Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, who were the capacities that formed the seeds through the establishment of karmic connections.
"Guidance" (*dao*) refers to the Tathāgata’s skillful inducement; "mind" (*xin*) refers to the emotional attachments of sentient beings. [These] are combined.

"Clarifying" refers to sentient beings who are attached in various places; it means to lead them so that they may attain liberation. There is nothing that does not reach them, and all [the terms] are used in a reverse manner to reveal this truth.
It is said that those who are currently receptive to the influence of this great transformation were all those who established karmic connections and formed seeds in the past.
Only then can one seize the opportunity to reform abuses and guide the mind until it reaches this state.

If it were not for past conditions, by what means could this have been achieved? Thus it is said: "There is nothing with which to guide the mind. This concludes the section on negative illustration. II. The Main Exposition has two parts: 1.

The main exposition of the ripening of the capacity; 2. The main exposition of the arrival of the teaching. Regarding the first: (The negative illustration proceeds from the teaching to the capacity, whereas the main exposition proceeds from the capacity to the teaching; this is certainly due to the mutual dependence of the literary structure.)
It also serves as an introduction to the master’s subtle eloquence.
Thus, when the Immortal Garden (Xuan-yuan) was completed, the capacities [of beings] were distinguished into the categories of small and great.

The two characters "so yi" (therefore) are terms that承接 (receive what precedes) and 引起 (introduce what follows); their meaning extends to the subsequent sections, while the preceding text has already clarified the matter.

When the teaching reaches those whose faculties are matured, the phrasing appears paradoxical and is difficult to comprehend logically; therefore, [the text] provides a general introduction to clarify it through a formal exposition.
"The Garden of the Immortals" (Siddhārthavana) is a place name, a site where ancient sages practiced the Way;
it is also called the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva), as an ancient king once raised deer there. This is where the Tathāgata, after twenty-one days, taught for the sake of the five bhikṣus and others.
This is the place where the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths was turned. To bring all matters to their ultimate conclusion is called "announcing completion" (*gàochéng*).

Here, we take the single assembly at the Immortal Garden (*xiānyuàn*) as the point when the teaching and listening reached their conclusion. "Faculties" (*jī*) refers to the spiritual capacities and natures of sentient beings; "analyzing" (*fēn*) means that the Tathāgata analyzed them.

It is said that at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, the Tathāgata directly proclaimed his original intent; although there were differences in the capacities of beings, he made no distinction between them.

However, when he reached the completion of his teaching in the Garden of the Immortals, because the five men heard the Dharma and attained deliverance, he then reflected that capacities differ and that the teachings must not bypass their respective stages.
Consequently, he analyzed them through his skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*): those of lesser capacity he led by means of the Lesser Vehicle.
The Way: the Great guides by means of the Great Dharma, each according to their own kind; thus, there is said to be a distinction between the small and the great.
The Preface cites this precisely to reveal that past conditions have varying depths, which is why capacities and natures differ as small or great.
Although they differ as small or great, ultimately it is due to those past conditions that one's mind can be guided. This is what is meant by "it is not [possible] without the past."
"It is indeed true that there is nothing better than relying [on the teachings] to guide the mind. △ Second, the explicit clarification of the arrival of the teaching.
At the Bequeathed Charge at the Golden River (*Suvarṇanadī*), the Path is distinguished by the categories of the Half and the Full [Teachings].
"Golden River" is the name of a river; in Sanskrit it is *Ariḷavati*, which here means "Possessing Gold," because within the river...

Because it is golden. It is located within the jurisdiction of the city of Kuśinagara, by the riverbank where there are twin *śāla* trees; this is precisely the place where the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa.
"Gù" (顧) means to look back; "mìng" (命) means a command. This is like the testament and admonitions of King Cheng at the end of his life.
It is called the "Bequeathed Charge" (*gùmìng*), which refers to the final instructions given by one who is about to depart.

Thus, after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, when the Tathāgata proceeded to the Twin Trees (*śālavana*) and preached the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*—upholding the *Vinaya* and discussing the Eternal—it was his final testament; therefore, it is also termed the "Bequeathed Charge.

"Dao" (the Way) refers to principle (*li*), indicating the doctrinal principles of the entire dispensation. "Shu" (distinction) means differentiation; it signifies that the Tathāgata [differentiated]...
Judgment: Regarding the two terms "half" (*ardha*) and "full" (*pūrṇa*), the text originates from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The sūtra states: "For example, a householder has an only son.

Fearing that he will not achieve success quickly, he diligently teaches him the 'half-syllables' day and night, but does not teach him the *Vyākaraṇa* (this is translated as 'the root of syllables,' being the foundation of all worldly writing;
this refers to the 'full-syllables'). This is because the child is young and his strength is not yet sufficient. This is just like...
When [the Buddha] came to the Golden River to deliver his final testament, he categorized the entire body of the teachings and principles into two divisions: the "Half" and the "Full.

His intention was that the ninefold scriptures of the Hīnayāna do not exhaust the full meaning of the Dharma and are thus like the "half-syllables," whereas the twelvefold scriptures of the Mahāyāna perfectly realize the nature of the mind and are thus like the "full-syllables. This refers to the classification of a single scripture.
The judgment is that the *pāramitā* (Full) and *hinayāna* (Partial) teachings each have their respective categories.

The Master of the Preface cites this precisely to reveal that it was through forty years of cultivation under the Great Sage’s guidance—nurtured by both the *pāramitā* and *hinayāna* vehicles—that he was finally able to break open the confinement of ordinary beings and transform the narrow-minded attachments of those of small capacity, so that all may become enlightened spirits and gather at Vulture Peak.
This is what is meant by the saying: "Without the Great Sage, there would be no way [to achieve this]."

The transformation [of beings] is indeed certain. The section on "Correct Elucidation" concludes. △ Third, preventing questions, which has two parts: first, preventing the question that the teaching has not yet arrived;

second, preventing the question that the capacity [of the audience] is not yet mature. Regarding the first: [Question: Since the Great Sage appeared in the world and employed both the "Half" and "Full" teachings to refine and cultivate [beings], it seems as though the time has come for the teaching to be mounted upon.

Why, then, is it that as soon as the Two Wisdoms are raised, the Three Stopping and One Contemplation are applied with such urgency? Is it not the case that the teaching has still not reached the time when it can be mounted? [Response to prevent this objection: ... (The text continues with the response).
"Is it not the case that when the teaching covers the period of the vehicle (*yāna*), there is nothing sufficient to scrutinize its sublime convergence?

'Is it not' (*qǐfēi*) is a term used for reverse illumination; it is equivalent to saying 'it is precisely. 'Teaching' (*jiào*) refers to the instruction from before. 'Covers' (*bèi*) means to reach or extend to.

'The period of the vehicle' (*chéngshí*) refers to the time when one may ride upon it. This means that since the past, there has already been transformation through both the Half-Teaching (*xiǎnmiào*) and the Full-Teaching (*fǎmén*)."
Having provided this instruction, it is now the time for practice; thus the Sūtra says, "Now is precisely that time. "Unfit" (wúzú) means, as the expression goes, "incapable.
"Examination" (hè) refers to investigation and scrutiny—specifically, examining through the subtle to expose the false and lead one into the true.

"The sublime assembly" refers specifically to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* searches out the ultimate reality and far transcends all other assemblies—being something that those who are false and deceitful cannot enter—this phrase intends to address those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

It means that since the time for their deliverance has arrived following the previous instructions, one should then preach the Dharma according to reality; however, there was concern that within the assembly there were still those who harbored increased pride.
The stream of those with overweening pride is incapable of having their falsehoods scrutinized; thus, they are led into the true and sublime assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
This is why the Tathāgata paused three times and did not preach [the Dharma]. II. Guarding against faculties that are as yet immature. (Question:

Since these are past affinities and they have already passed through both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, it seems their faculties must be mature. Why, then, at the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter, were there five thousand members of the assembly who withdrew, and why did the five hundred disciples only receive their predictions after the three turnings? Is it not the case that their faculties are still immature?)
Is there anyone who has not yet reached maturity? (As Yantou Fafang said:

We know that the five thousand who withdrew from their seats were those whose arrogance increased as they advanced; the five hundred who received their predictions were those who together honored the traces of the esoteric transformation.
This "knower" refers back to the meaning of the maturation of the spiritual capacity (*indriya*).

It means that because of this maturation of capacity, one comes to know that the departure of the five thousand [monks] from their seats was not literal, and that the bestowal of predictions upon the five hundred was entirely intentional (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*). Regarding the departure of the five thousand:
after Śāriputra had made his three requests in the "Expedient Means" chapter, and the Tathāgata had granted permission to provide a detailed explanation, at that time—four... [text fragment ends].
Among the assembly, there were five thousand people who rose from their seats and withdrew.
"Those who advance" refers to those who advance through actual practice while increasing their arrogance, leading others to follow them in withdrawing.

Those who increase their arrogance merely possess superior aspirations with which they look down on others, yet lack superior conduct for self-cultivation; as the Sūtra says, they have not attained what they claim.
This refers to those who have attained [realization] yet claim they have not, and those who have not realized it yet claim they have. "Chou" (儔) means "class" or "kind.

This implies that since there are such individuals, there must necessarily be a group of followers belonging to that same class. As the Sūtra says: "These people have meager merit and are incapable of receiving this Dharma.
Therefore, five thousand people withdrew. On one hand, it was to avoid the fault of slandering the Dharma; on the other...

Thus, while it may seem to hinder others from hearing the Dharma, it actually accords with reality; while appearing to cause harm, it brings hidden benefit. How could this truly be an act of arrogance?

As for the "five hundred," these are the five hundred disciples mentioned in the section on the prediction of future enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), namely Kāuṇḍinya, the three Kāśyapas, and so forth, up to Cunda and Svāgata. Regarding their "receiving the prediction," this refers to their reception of the teaching...
They received the Tathāgata’s prediction. The Sūtra states: "Those five hundred bhikṣus shall successively become Buddhas. It further says:

"We have heard the unsurpassed sound of the prediction of peace and security, just as the Tathāgata bestowed it. The meaning of these five hundred receiving [the prediction] is that they reverently practiced [the path].
As for "secret transformation," it refers to secretly manifesting [the teaching] to those of inferior faculties in order to transform their kindred.

"Traces" refers to outward manifestations. When it is said that the five hundred disciples received predictions despite being of inferior capacity, this does not mean they were truly of inferior capacity;
rather, these are all merely traces of their reverent practice and secret transformation.

Based on this, the five thousand and five hundred [disciples] cannot be judged by their words or appearances. (Question: In the passage concerning the prediction for those of inferior capacity, there was previously Pūrṇa and the twelve hundred, followed later by Ānanda and the two thousand. Now, specifically...)

As for the statement regarding "five hundred," what does it mean? The answer is: in the passage concerning Pūrṇa receiving his prediction, it is explicitly stated that he was "secretly a bodhisattva while outwardly appearing as a śrāvaka. From this, it can be known that his faculties had matured.

Furthermore, although Ānanda’s rank was still that of one in training (*śaikṣa*), the Tathāgata clearly stated that he had awakened the aspiration for enlightenment at the time of King Gaganagañja Buddha; thus, his faculties having matured can likewise be known. As for the remaining two thousand people, since they belonged to the stage of those in training, there is no cause for doubt even though they received their predictions among those of inferior faculties.

As for the twelve hundred people and the others who were not present at this assembly, there is even less cause for doubt. However, these five hundred disciples, being of the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and yet present at the current assembly, did not receive a prediction during either the discourse on the Dharma or the discourse through parables. They must therefore belong to the same category of those with inferior faculties who await the explanation of the causes and conditions.

He has only now received his prediction of enlightenment. Fearing that others might suspect his spiritual capacity (*indriya*) was still immature, he specifically raised this matter as a precaution). This concludes the preliminary account of the circumstances for preaching the sutra.

△ Second, the formal exposition of the primary purpose of the sutra. (Regarding the "primary purpose" (*śāstra-artha*): it refers to the critical junctures where the essential points are struck; it is not a sequential introduction covering the beginning and end of the entire sutra, nor is it an introduction following a step-by-step progression from section to section.)

I have merely used the analogy of a dragonfly skimming the water to enable students to grasp the essential principles of the teaching; therefore, I dare not add "snake's feet" [superfluous commentary] to this current exposition. Nevertheless, lecturers must not consider this a deficiency, nor need they feel compelled to force a comprehensive synthesis or inclusion of all points. This is divided into five parts: First, the Purpose of the Introductory Section; Second, the Purpose of the Exposition of the Dharma; Third, the Purpose of the Exposition by Simile; Fourth, the Purpose of the Section on Causes and Conditions; Fifth, the Purpose of the Manifestation of Benefits. First: The purpose of the Introductory Section is to provide a general overview of the scripture’s intent and to establish the foundation for the subsequent teachings. It serves to inspire faith and resolve in those who have not yet developed them, to deepen the faith and resolve of those who already possess them, and to clarify the ultimate goal of the Buddha’s appearance in the world. Furthermore, it reveals that the Tathāgata’s preaching of the *Lotus Sūtra* is not a mere incidental occurrence, but rather the fulfillment of his original vow to bring all sentient beings to the single vehicle (*ekayāna*).

It also demonstrates that the Buddha’s teaching is not limited to a single lifetime, but is the continuous manifestation of his eternal, unconditioned body throughout the three periods of time. Thus, the Introductory Section functions as the gateway through which the profound meaning of the entire sūtra is revealed. (Note: The following sections—Exposition of the Dharma, Exposition by Simile, Causes and Conditions, and Manifestation of Benefits—are to be understood according to their respective contexts within the sūtra. First: The Purpose of the Introductory Section. Second: The Purpose of the Exposition of the Dharma. Third: The Purpose of the Exposition by Simile. Fourth: The Purpose of the Causes and Conditions. Fifth: The Purpose of the Manifestation of Benefits. First: [The Introductory Section].
The reason for emitting light and manifesting auspicious omens is to open up the source of the teaching that invites [the Buddha].
The two characters "so yi" (the reason why) refer back to the statement that the teaching has reached the point where the capacity [of the disciples] has matured.

It is precisely because the teaching has reached the point where the capacity has matured—at the very moment of making the request—that light is emitted to open the source of this teaching. As for "emitting," it proceeds from within.
"Externally": the principle of expanding from the narrow to the broad, and extending from the near to the distant. "Light" refers to the white tuft (*ūrṇā-kośa*) between the eyebrows.

Regarding "the light of the marks," the Sūtra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One emitted the light of the mark of the white tuft between his eyebrows, illuminating eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction," and so forth.
"Manifesting auspicious omens" refers to the signs manifested within the light. The Sūtra says: "All saw those... [and so on].

The land; the sentient beings of the six realms; furthermore, seeing the Buddhas currently residing in those lands and hearing the sūtras, dharmas, and so forth taught by those Buddhas—these are such [things].
Now, as for this radiant sign being called an auspicious omen (*śubhanimitta*), it is because it serves as a portent for the exposition of this present sūtra;
thus, it "opens" [the way]. "To request" means to raise a question; that is, within the sūtra, Maitreya beholds the light.
"Omen" (*śubha-nimitta*) refers to Mañjuśrī’s inquiry. "Instruction" (*deśanā*) has the meaning of "guidance.
Since the Tathāgata emits light from the front and Maitreya issues his request from behind, the emission of light serves as the true introduction and precursor to the request.

"Source" (*mūla*) has the meaning of "origin. Since the Tathāgata manifests omens to suit the capacities of sentient beings and Maitreya stirs his thoughts to issue a request, [the manifestation of omens...]

Furthermore, the auspicious signs open up the occasion for the request. If, at that time, the Buddha had not emitted light and manifested these signs, Maitreya would have had no basis to raise questions or make a request;
even the Great Wisdom Mañjuśrī would have been forced to remain silent with his tongue clamped shut.
Thus, what is described by these two lines truly constitutes the essential purport of the introduction (*nidāna*). II. The Essential Purport of the Dharma-Exposition.
Emerging from Samādhi to Proclaim Virtue: Expounding the Vast Strategy of the Buddha’s Wisdom.

"Emerging from samādhi" is said in contrast to entering samādhi during the introductory section (*nidāna*). In the introductory section, because the great capacity [of the audience] was unmoving, it was necessary to enter samādhi in order to move them.
Now, because this great capacity is about to be activated, it is necessary to emerge from samādhi.
He brings it forth. Its emergence and entry are both established through expedient means (*upāya*). In the Buddha, fundamentally, there is neither emergence nor entry.
As the Sūtra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One arose calmly from samādhi. This is the textual passage concerning emerging from meditative concentration (*samāpatti*).

"To manifest" (*yang*) means to praise and extol. "Virtue" (*de*) refers to the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate. As the Sūtra says: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable. Its...
"The gate of wisdom" and "difficult to understand and difficult to enter," etc., are passages that extol its virtues (*guṇa*).

One speaks of "virtues" rather than "wisdom" because wisdom constitutes a specific entity, whereas virtue is a general designation; the intent is to include the specific within the general. Furthermore, that which is fully realized within oneself is called a "virtue.
This is because both the provisional and ultimate wisdoms are the principles (*tattva*) realized by the Tathāgata. There are two ways of explaining this.
I. To Proclaim Fully: By means of the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate, sentient beings equally possess [these qualities], yet they are deluded and do not know them.
Now, emerging from samādhi to manifest his virtues, he truly proclaims them so that they may be known. II. To Expand Fully:

By means of Buddha-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*) and Buddha-intelligence (*buddhaprajñā*), for forty years he has suppressed them within his breast. Now, emerging from samādhi to manifest his virtues, he truly expands what was held within his breast. Buddha-intelligence...
This refers to what is stated in the sutras: "The Buddha knows, the Buddha sees," "all-aspect wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*), and so forth; these are merely different names for the same meaning.
"Makuroku" (弘略) means "great and vast. This indicates that although there are various designations such as "the Buddha knows, the Buddha sees" and so on hereafter, [they all refer to this].
This reveals the Buddha’s wisdom. It is based on the meaning of the two types of knowledge—the provisional and the real—presented at the beginning of the chapter on "Non-Emergence.

Thus, by emerging from meditative concentration and extolling his virtues, he has already fully unfolded the general outline of the Buddha’s wisdom. Even if the World-Honored One had not emerged from concentration to extol his virtues, [the meaning would remain the same].
The assembly had no way to voice their doubts; Śāriputra had no way to make his triple request; and the Tathāgata had no way to provide a detailed explanation.
Even if those of the highest faculties were present in the assembly, they could do nothing but gape at the Dragon Gate. Thus it is described in these two lines.
Is this not the teaching of the fundamental principle through the Dharma? △ Third, the teaching of the fundamental principle through parables.
The phrase "decaying house" serves as the general gateway for entering the Great [Vehicle].
The two characters "decaying house" refer collectively to the entire text of this single parable. "Decaying" refers to the appearance of ruin and instability; "house" [refers to the three realms].
This refers to the place of reliance and entrustment; its meaning is illustrated by the metaphor of the three realms being devoid of peace, as sentient beings rely upon them.
As the Sūtra says: "In a kingdom, city, or village, there was a great elder... This is the metaphor of the dilapidated house.
It is also called the "burning house" because it is consumed by a great fire. What is here termed "dilapidated" refers to the fact that the house has long been worn out and decrepit.
"To clear" means to remove obstructions; when there is something obstructed, one clears it so that it may flow through.

"Entering the Great" still refers to the meaning of "converging the Small into the Great" found in the section on the Dharma-exposition (*dharmaparyāya*). The term "pattern" (*wen*) originates from the *Zhongyong*; "pattern" refers to the strokes and dots of written characters.
"Tracks" refer to the ruts of a carriage. It is said that "the carriages share the same tracks and the scripts share the same characters";
this means that the regulations established by the Duke of Wen and the Duke of Wu remain such that no one in the world today dares to deviate from them.

Taking this as an analogy, the method of explaining the chapters—whereby the Small Vehicle is integrated into the Great Vehicle—is the immutable standard of all Buddhas, just like the uniformity of the script and the tracks of carriages.

It is similar; however, because the explanation of the Dharma was so profound and subtle that it reached only those of superior faculties, it conversely revealed that the textual method was obstructed and did not penetrate to those of middling or inferior capacities.

Therefore, the parable of the decaying house was taught, using the shallowness of the three carts and the single cart to illustrate the depth of the three vehicles and the one path, so that hearers might understand the Dharma through the metaphor.
This precisely clarifies the preceding chapter, removing its profound subtleties and obstructions.

The meaning of this is as follows: If the Tathāgata had not explained it with clarity, even those four individuals of medium capacity would not have recognized the sequence of the Great and Small Vehicles, nor their relative depth and shallowness;
how then could they have fully heard the single, perfectly integrated sound and obtained the benefit of receiving their prediction?
This parable exhaustively conveys the essential purport of the first week of the teaching. △ Fourth, the Essential Purport of the *Nidāna-parivarta*.
The "Transformed City" (Gandharva-nagara) preserves the continuity of past conditions so they do not fall away; the "Tied Jewel" clarifies that the rational nature is ever-present.

The two characters for "Transformed City" refer generally to the entire text of this chapter. It is called "transformed" (*hua*) because it suddenly exists where there was nothing; it is called a "city" (*cheng*) because it prevents wrongdoing and wards off enemies.
In meaning, it is a metaphor for the provisional establishment of the *Hīnayāna*, which can prevent the wrongs of *dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*, and ward off the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence).

Because it is an adversary [to the teaching]. The Sūtra states: "The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: 'In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū,' and so forth. This is the text from the "Chapter on the Phantom City" (*Gandavyūha*).
"To lead" (*yin*) means to guide and attract. "Past conditions" refers to the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū; it indicates the re-establishment of karmic connections through the preaching.

The opportunity for this has already slipped away, as if lost. Within the preceding two weeks, those of the superior and middle faculties have all attained understanding and received their predictions;

only those of inferior faculties remain. Although they possess past conditions, they have not yet been able to achieve awakening. If the Tathāgata did not guide them, these past conditions would be lost.
For this reason, he further taught the chapter on the "City of Transformation," causing each of them to recognize their former lives.

This is the cause. Furthermore, one knows the stage in which one dwells and is close to the Buddha-wisdom; it is precisely for this reason that one leads those with whom one formed karmic connections in the past, ensuring they do not fall away.
The two characters "tied" (xi) and "jewel" (zhu) collectively refer to the entire metaphor. "Tied" means to bind or secure.
The "jewel" refers to the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*). This means that a wealthy relative, out of compassion for a poor friend, ties a wish-fulfilling gem inside the latter's garment;

this is a metaphor for how the Tathāgata, having established karmic connections in the past, has placed the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) of sentient beings.
The Sūtra says: "For example, there was a man who went to the house of a close friend and lay down after drinking wine.
At that time, the friend had business to attend to at the government office, so he tied a priceless jewel inside the man's garment. This is the passage concerning the parable of tying the jewel.

"The Illuminator" (Mingzhe) describes the meaning of its fulfillment: the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect wisdom), which is eternally present—meaning it is never absent.

This is an error. To say that those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), at the time they were first transformed by the Buddha in the past, already made the vow for omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), means that the seeds of such knowledge had already been sown within the field of consciousness (*vijñāna-kṣetra*).
However, because they subsequently regressed from the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) toward the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), they considered themselves to have lost their portion [of Buddhahood].

In meaning, this appears to be an error. Now, hearing these causal conditions, they suddenly awaken to their past causes and personally receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), thereby experiencing great joy.

Beyond expectation, both [the Buddha and the disciples] speak of the same parable of the tied jewel. The intent is that because the jewel within the garment exists, it serves to describe and establish the rational nature of consciousness’s reception;

it has remained ever-present until now, never having been lost from the beginning. However, if the Tathāgata did not provide guidance and lead them forth, those of inferior capacity would have no means to receive their prediction of enlightenment.
And if the five hundred had not described and established this, the Tathāgata’s bestowal of it would have been in vain.
Therefore, in order to connect this with the momentum of the *chengling* (the "commanding" section), I have summarized the meaning and set it forth as a preface.
Thus, the master of the preface may be said to have profoundly grasped the essential tenets of the entire cycle of causes and conditions. △ Fifth, revealing the benefits of the essential tenets.
The phrase "digging a well" demonstrates the manifold methods of awakening.
These two characters, "digging a well," also serve as a metaphor for the entire text. "Digging a well" refers to exerting effort to excavate the earth to form a well in search of water;
this meaning serves as a metaphor for a Bodhisattva’s cultivation of practice to sever delusions, seeking bodhi by awakening to true emptiness. Sūtra.
It says: "For example, suppose there is a person who, parched with thirst and needing water, digs a well in a high plateau to seek it.

This is the analogy of digging a well. "Manifesting" (*xian*) means to reveal clearly; it refers to employing various methods of instruction and enlightenment so that people may come to know [the truth].
It speaks of the efficacy of this sutra. "Instruction" (*shi*) means pointing out, and "enlightenment" (*wu*) means awakening. The Sutra says: "All bodhi..."
All [beings] attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* all belong to this sutra; this clearly demonstrates that this sutra provides many methods for awakening. Furthermore, it says:
"This sutra opens the gate of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*) and reveals the true aspect (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*)," which precisely demonstrates that this sutra points toward many directions.
Thus, the single metaphor of digging a well serves as a comprehensive illustration of the places where this sutra points and the places where it awakens; these are indeed numerous.
Through these skillful means, may everyone come to know and uphold [this teaching], and may each individual internalize it without forgetting.
Thus, from the conclusion of the three cycles of the Dharma, the records for the three capacities have been perfected;

furthermore, by extensively recording the present and prophesying the future, those who were precisely the ones to be saved have all already been saved, and even for those not yet saved, the causes and conditions for their salvation have been established.
Following this parable of the well-digging, there are eighteen and a half fascicles of scripture.
Although they appear somewhat repetitive and interconnected, they are nothing other than an extensive manifestation of the supreme benefits of this sutra, intended to ensure its transmission.

One must understand that these various supreme benefits do not, in essence, transcend the manifold methods of "showing" and "awakening"; thus, the single parable of the well-digging is truly sufficient to manifest them all.

Increasing the Essential Meaning. This concludes the formal exposition of the essential meaning of this single sutra. △ Third, the conclusion and praise of the excellence of the teaching and the profundity of the capacity [of the audience], in two parts:

First, concluding the sutra and praising the teaching; Second, concluding the upholding [of the teaching] and praising the capacity. The first part has two sections: First, concluding that the sutra is remote; Second, praising the excellence of the conditions for the teaching. The first section: [The text continues with the specific content of the first section.]
The words and their meanings are perfectly distinct; the metaphors presented are solely for the sake of clarity.

"Words" (*śabda*) refer to the expressive phrases and terminology; "meanings" (*artha*) refer to the principles and logic expressed by those words. "Perfectly distinct" (*vyanjana*) signifies that which is vivid and clearly manifest.
This concludes the brief summary of the general outline, intended to allow one to recognize the fundamental tenets. As for the remaining words and meanings, they follow accordingly.
All are clearly and vividly present; this can be seen within the sutras. "Metaphor" (yù) means to provide an illustration; "elucidation" (chén) means to set forth in detail.

When it is said that the words and meanings within the sutras are vivid and clear, it is because they are nothing other than illustrations and detailed expositions intended to make known subtle and profound meanings that are otherwise remote and difficult to grasp.
"Only" (wéi) means "solely. Master Zhu Wen-gong said: "The 'sole' refers to that which people do not know."
As for the ground known only to oneself, now in this sutra, only the Buddha has fully realized it;
all others do not know it, and thus it is also termed "unique" (*eka*). This conveys the sense of being so remote that it cannot be reached.

Although the words and their meanings are perfectly clear, that which is explained and elaborated therein is in fact truly remote and impossible to fathom or attain. This indeed reveals the excellence of this sutra.
These words are concise yet rich in meaning; they serve to show that the Tathāgata’s elucidations and expositions were not for minor causes.
△ Second, praising the excellence of the conditions for the teaching.

Were it not for Great Compassion that universally rescues and uproots those submerged in the stagnant currents, and for the Ultimate Compassionate Heart that saves those who have lost their true nature in confusion and darkness, this would be nothing but solitary.
"Solitary" is used here as a term of contrast to clarify the meaning; it signifies that the words and meanings of this sutra are thus perfectly complete and manifest, serving as a metaphor.
Chen Rushi’s [critique] is merely superficial. All of these [teachings] originate from the Tathāgata’s great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and vast salvation;
they are the ultimate intent of his singularly profound pity to rescue those mired in the depths and to uplift those who are deluded and unconscious.

However, the author of the preface did not wish to state this directly, and thus used terms such as "solely non-[Buddhist]" (*dufei*) to reveal it through indirect implication. "Great compassion and vast salvation" praises the Buddha’s heart of loving-kindness; "pity" (*ai*) refers to—
The meaning of *ci* (compassion) is unobstructed compassion that universally covers all; thus it is called "Great Pity" (*dà'āi*). The meaning of *kuàng* (vast) is distance;
it is boundless compassion that rescues many beings over a long duration; thus it is called "Vast Rescue. The meaning of *bá* (to pull out) is to save and deliver.

Those who are "stuck and submerged in the current" refers to those of the Two Vehicles (*er shèng*), for they are stuck in provisional teachings and submerged in the Lesser Path, like one clutching a stone [and sinking].
Regarding the flow of those submerged in the abyss, the sutras speak of the Dharma of the three cycles and the bestowal of predictions for the three faculties;

this is precisely for the purpose of rescuing such persons. First, "supreme compassion" (*ekāntika-karuṇā*): it praises the Buddha’s compassionate mindfulness, wherein his compassion of same-nature (*sahaja-karuṇā*) is equal, one, and non-dual;
therefore, it is called "one. His unconditioned compassion (*apratyaya-karuṇā*) reaches the ultimate and is without limit; therefore, it is called "supreme. As for "rescuing":...
Regarding the meaning of "guiding and introducing": those who are "confused and have lost their nature" refers to ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists.
Because ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists are obscured by ignorance and deluded by false views, they are like people who have lost their senses out of fear for their heads.

The sūtras extensively record this regarding the present and provide prophetic declarations regarding the future precisely for the purpose of guiding and introducing such individuals. Based on this, every word and every phrase is compassionate and poignant.
With a heart full of grief, I offer this single verse and single line, containing my bitter tears. May those who see or hear it likewise respectfully embody the Sage’s intention.

This concludes the section on the conclusion of the sutra and the praise of the teaching. △ Second, the conclusion regarding the capacity for upholding and praising, which has two parts: first, the conclusion on the flourishing of upholding;
second, the praise for the profundity of the causal capacity. Regarding the first:

From the Han dynasty to the Tang, over six hundred years have passed; throughout this period, one has examined more than four thousand fascicles across all the various scriptures, yet none has been as widely upheld and practiced as this sutra.
Since the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty during the Yongping era, the Buddha-dharma first entered China; hence it is said "from the Han.
Although the Master did not specifically examine the dates and years when he composed this preface, it must have been during the early Tang period; hence it is said "until the Tang.
In the interim, it passed through the Eastern and Western Jin dynasties, the Northern and Southern courts, and the Sui dynasty—approximately six [dynasties].

"Over a hundred years. This refers to the collective statement of the *zongtong* (presiding director). "Successive transmissions" refers to the historical lineage. "Various records" (*qunji*) refers to the many scriptures;
the four thousand or more fascicles (*zhou*) mentioned below represent the total number of various scriptures transmitted during the interval between the Han and Tang dynasties.

"Fascicle" (*zhou*) is synonymous with "scroll" (*juan*). In modern times, characters are often written as *zhou* instead of *juan*, and ancient scriptures were likewise so. Therefore, the editor of the preface has retained [the term].
The *Sāmmatīya-śāstra* states: Between the Tang and Han dynasties, more than two hundred individuals—both monastics and laypeople—translated scriptures from Sanskrit into Chinese.
The resulting Tripitaka consists of one thousand four hundred and eighty works in eight thousand four hundred and seventy-six fascicles.
Since the destruction by fire during the Wei and Zhou periods, much has been lost; of those currently included in the canon, there are eight [remaining].
There are one hundred and seventy-four sections and four thousand two hundred and fifty-three fascicles; thus it is said there are "more than four thousand scrolls.
Regarding the two characters *shouchi* (upholding), there are both general and specific meanings. Generally speaking, they encompass reading, reciting, explaining, transcribing, and making offerings.

Each of these was received and maintained. To discuss them individually: "receiving" (*śīla*) refers to grasping their meaning, while "maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*) refers to reciting and upholding their texts.

This indicates their flourishing and preeminence. From the Han to the Tang dynasties, over a span of more than six hundred years, it is said that the total number of various scriptures transmitted amounted to over four thousand fascicles (*pustaka*).
Among those, none surpassed [the Prajñāpāramitā] in the flourishing of its reception and maintenance.

This sutra is intended to firmly manifest the extraordinary power and excellence of this scripture; furthermore, it shows that there have long been those among sentient beings who are capable of receiving and upholding it.
△ Second, praising the profundity of the causal conditions of the capacity [to receive].

Is this not the convergence of the Dharma and the faculties, and the lingering dust of the wisdom of the Victorious One? Upon hearing it, one feels profound reverence; is it not the remaining achievement of King Kubera?

"Jiang fei" (will it not be) shares the same meaning as "zi fei" (it is certainly not) mentioned above. This indicates that the upholding and practice of this sutra is flourishing and surpasses the six hundred [other teachings].

That which is recorded in the various scriptures all arises from the mutual resonance between the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) and the teaching (*śāsana*). Upon hearing it, one develops profound reverence;

for all are but the lingering traces left by the Victorious One of Wisdom (*Jñānavijaya*), and all belong to the remaining achievements of the Majestic King (*Māhārāja*). Therefore, they also employ terms such as "about to be non-existent" (*yāng-fei*) to reveal this through contrast.

"Capacity" (*ji*) refers to the person who receives and upholds [the teaching]; "teaching" (*jiao*) is this present sutra; "resonance" (*kou*) means striking together. This signifies that when such a person encounters [it]—
This sutra strikes at the heart, such that one cannot forget it; "and likewise" (*bing tong*) means the same.

"Zhi-sheng yi-chen" (智勝遺塵) refers to the karmic conditions established during the Great Pervasive [Kalpa] (*da-tong*). "Yi" means what remains; "chen" means traces. It speaks of the karmic conditions established during the Great Pervasive Kalpa.

As for those who have matured and attained liberation during the interim, their number is unknown. Those whose faculties and the teaching now strike one another in resonance are likewise those with whom Śākyamuni formed karmic bonds through his supreme wisdom.
It is specifically because there remain traces from that interim period that have not yet been liberated;

were it not for such a karmic affinity, how could it be that as soon as the faculty and the teaching encounter one another, they strike so resonantly in the heart that one cannot forget them? This is why, upon hearing [of him], one feels profound reverence.
Once it passes through the faculty of hearing, body and mind take refuge [in it], unable to bear casting it aside; this is the meaning [of the text].

"The remaining legacy of King Wei" refers to the capacity for forming karmic connections during the time of King Wei-yin; "remaining" (yú) is synonymous with "leftover" (yí), and "legacy" (jì) means "merit" (gōng).

It implies that among those who formed karmic connections during the time of King Wei-yin, the number of those who subsequently obtained benefit and reaped merit is beyond measure. If even now, upon hearing this, one feels deep reverence...
These [beings] all established karmic conditions during the time of Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja; they are specifically the remaining merits not yet gathered during the intervening period.
Were it not for such conditions, how could one pass through the faculty of hearing but once and immediately cause body and mind to take refuge, unable to bear to let go?

Based on this, it is difficult to encounter [the Dharma] without cause; only through specific conditions can one become intimate with it. Those who have fortunately seen or heard it should not fail themselves by neglecting their past conditions. Thus it is said.

The conclusion of the Sūtra’s essential purport. △ Third, the prayer and exposition of the intent, in two parts: first, the prayer at the beginning of the sequence; second, the praise of the Sūtra and exposition of the intent. Regarding the first:

I have briefly set forth this preface at the head of the Sūtra to synthesize its meaning, so that one may quickly purify the six sense faculties and look up toward the auspicious assembly of the Compassionate Honored One.

The profound method for swiftly accomplishing the four virtues and proceeding to the Land of Bliss consists of two initial lines that clarify the introduction (*nidāna*). "Sudden" (*jù*) refers to the very beginning of the sutra;

"introduction" (*xù*) means to describe the general outline, while "comprehensive" (*zǒng*) means to summarize the essential meaning. The purport of the introduction is that it is already known that [the Buddha] has received and upheld this sutra.
This belongs to the capacity of those who possess the majestic power of Universal Victory; therefore, although I am not quick-witted, I dare not abandon myself.
Suddenly, a superior resolve was aroused within me, and I have thus set forth the general outline before this sutra, summarizing its essential meaning.

Furthermore, the term "zhé" (輒) carries the meaning of acting with haste or impulsiveness. The intention is that because the *Lotus Sūtra* is so venerable and sublime, it is not easy to place one's words at its head;

thus, to have conceived the thought of composing a preface was truly beyond self-measurement. Therefore, he says "impulsively" (*zhé yú*) and so forth—this is also the Great Master’s expression of humility.

The final four lines are a prayer of aspiration, using "shù dé" (庶得) in the sense of "perhaps" or "may it be so. This conveys the meaning of not daring to decide for oneself. The intended meaning is as follows:

The reason I have ventured to compose this preface is simply because the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are firmly bound, auspicious encounters are difficult to meet, the four virtues (*caturguṇa*) are deficient, and the profound Way (*gambhīra-mārga*) cannot be pursued.
Perhaps by means of this slight cause, one may attain the early purification of the six sense-faculties—and so forth.
"Early purification" means being pure right here and now, without waiting for a later time. This is the merit of the Dharma Master.

The Chapter on Virtues states: "Good sons and good daughters, if they read, recite, explain, or transcribe [this sutra], they shall obtain eight hundred merits of the eye, up to twelve hundred merits of the mind.

By these merits, they shall adorn the six sense faculties, causing them all to be purified. The Preface Master took this as his basis; therefore, he prayed for the early purification of the six faculties, gazing upward in reverence.
"Also," "Hoping for," and "The Compassionate Honored One. The Compassionate Honored One refers to the World-Honored One;
for the World-Honored One treats the three realms with universal benevolence, like a mother’s compassion, viewing the four modes of birth as her only child, and is as venerable as a father.

"A Grand Assembly" refers to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak), because Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, with its multitude of eminent scholars, constitutes a magnificent and auspicious assembly of a single era. [This concludes the section on] distinguishing the merits.

The *Guṇaparyāya-parivarta* states: "If there are sons or daughters of good family who, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching that his lifespan is long and far-reaching, believe and understand it with a profound mind, they shall see the Buddha as always dwelling on Vulture Peak. The Preface takes this as its basis;
therefore, it prays for the auspicious assembly at the Spirit Mountain (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*). The *Āyuḥpramāṇa-parivarta* states: "I always dwell here, and by means of various supernormal powers, I..."
Sentient beings who are inverted do not see [him], even though he is near. Furthermore, it is said:
"Once sentient beings have gained faith and understanding, becoming upright and their minds supple, then I and the assembly of monks shall together emerge from Vulture Peak Mountain.

Based on this, the single assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly present to this day, never having dispersed; it is only because the six sense-faculties of sentient beings are so firmly bound that, although [the Buddha] is near, they do not see him.

This is seen in the text. This is why the Master of the Preface first prayed for the purification of his faculties; thus, there is a basis for his longing gaze toward the Compassionate Honored One at this auspicious assembly.

"Swift accomplishment" means that it is achieved through mindfulness alone, without requiring a long period of time. Regarding the "four virtues," the ancients referred to the four virtues such as permanence (*nitya*).

Now, following the *Da Cheng* (Mahāyāna-samparigraha), they refer to the Buddhas' protective mindfulness described in the "Chapter on Exhortation and Arousal" (*Pravartana-parivarta*), which plants [the seeds of] the multitude...

Virtuous root. Entering the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), one gives rise to the mind that seeks to save living beings. For the sake of the four virtues, the "Chapter on Exhortation" states:
"Good sons and good daughters, if you accomplish four dharmas, you will certainly obtain this sutra. The Master of the Preface takes this as his basis;
therefore, he prays for the swift accomplishment of these four virtues. "To proceed" means to seek. "Pure Land" refers to the West, because there [in that land] one only receives...
All things are blissful because they are free from all suffering. The profound principle may still be called the "wondrous path," referring to the *Lotus Sūtra* expounded by Amitābha.
The "Bhaiṣajyarāja" chapter states: "If a woman hears this sūtra and practices according to its teachings, at the end of her life here, she will be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
How could the Great Master—so majestic as a dragon or elephant—ever be inferior to women? It is based on this meaning [that he taught this].
Therefore, we pray for the profound principles of the Land of Bliss. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:

"In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha (translated here as 'Immeasurable Life'), who currently resides and expounds the Dharma. Based on this, the profound principles of the Land of Bliss can still be personally received even today;
it is only because sentient beings have deficiencies in the four virtues that they are unable to proceed there. This is why the Preface Master first...
I pray that virtue may be perfected; thus, one seeks the Pure Land, for the profound Way has its source therein. △ Second, praising the scripture and stating the intention:
Its extensive praise is inexhaustible, and it is said that it shall be perpetually bequeathed to future generations.
The first phrase praises the sutra for its vastness and magnificence. "Inexhaustible" means that its meaning cannot be fully fathomed.

The intention of the Preface is to state that one already knows that every word and every phrase of this sutra flows forth from the Tathāgata’s great compassion and universal salvation—his ultimate heart of pity.
However, I am ashamed that my wisdom is not like Mañjuśrī’s and my eloquence falls short of that of the heavenly maiden. Broadly...
To praise this sutra, even if one were to exhaust the surface of bamboo tablets, it would still be difficult to fully describe its merits. The following phrase expresses the intent [of the preface].
"Forever" means eternally. "Bequeathed" means left as a legacy. These are various particles. "Henceforth" refers to from this time forward until the very end of the future limit.

"Thus" (yun er) is a concluding particle; it is equivalent to saying, "This is precisely that meaning. The purport of the introduction is that such-and-such is the reason for propagating [the teaching].

To praise this sutra is to know its depths as boundless. It is merely intended to provide a single leaf for a small boat to cross ten thousand acres of surging waves, so that students may understand the sutra through its preface, extend themselves to others, and cause this Dharma-lamp to be passed from lamp to lamp and flame to flame, perpetually preserved until the end of the future. This is my hope.

This is all there is to it. The preface to the *Fahua Zhizhang Shu* (The Palm-Sized Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), which provides a comprehensive overview of the scripture, concludes here. [End of] the Phonetic Glossary.

*Fù* (to fall prostrate). *Póchā* (Sanskrit: *Virūpākṣa*; translated here as "Broad Eyes," the name of the Western Heavenly King). *Huá* (phoneticized as *hù bā*, pronounced like *huá*; meaning "disorderly" or "troublesome"). *Shùnshàn* (the second character is phoneticized as *shí zhàn*, pronounced like *shàn*;

Làng (meaning "unrefined" or "uncouth"; upper radical *mó*, level tone; pronunciation *mǎng*). Bò (pronounced *bǒ*; meaning "lame," referring to a partial impairment of the feet). Quó (pronounced *jué* in the level tone; meaning "a disease of the hands and feet").
